en: I shall now describe the sequence of consecration renowned within the mandala;
furthermore, a wise person should not strictly examine whether a candidate is worthy or unworthy.
There are some here in this life who are evildoers;
by beholding the mandala, may there be a destruction of their sins.
Furthermore, the characteristics of pure disciples are now described:
they are humble, possess all their limbs in full, and are always devoted to the Mahāyāna.
They are proficient in the applications of mantra and tantra, skilled in the arts and crafts,
constantly devoted to meditation and study, and entirely dedicated to devotion toward their guru.
What is meant by "nourishing"?
Those endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and vigor; those who do not indulge in sensual pleasures;
those free from anger and pride; and those who do not revile their teachers or gurus.
They are free from cruelty, pure-souled, having completely abandoned sinful thoughts;
they are devoid of broken speech and harshness, and are endowed with virtuous qualities.
To such excellent disciples— who have respectfully formed the maṇḍala, placed their knees upon the ground, and likewise held flowers and garlands in their hands— [he spoke].
To disciples who were free from prior attachments, stainless, worthy vessels of merit,
whose mental continuums were immersed in faith, and who were possessed of a longing for the Dharma;
Then, he should speak thus even to those worthy ones standing before him:
"Thou art the *samaya*, thou art the *samaya*; I am the *samaya*.
[I am] in the great and terrible *hāhetapana* hell, in the turbulent cold water."
O Queen, [he is reborn] in Mahātapanah,
Kukkula, Agnighaṭa, as well as in Mahāraurava and Raurava.
In Tapana, Raṭana, and Praraṭana, and in Avīci, which is characterized by cold, heat, and weapons—
those beings devoted to evil who have been born in these [hells].
In order to uplift them and establish them in perfect enlightenment,
and for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bliss, I perform this auspicious deed.
Regarding the accomplishment of the food:
having caused it to be recited three times and having performed the recitation of the mantra that ends with the word *vighnānta*, [one should offer] the food in this manner.
Having taken water, having sprinkled [the area], and having performed the protection, |||
Oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ phaṭ.
This protection mantra is empowered by reciting "Vighnāntakṛt" one hundred and eight times.
Then, the wise one should thus encourage them: [he should visualize] in the hearts of the disciples a thunderbolt born from the syllable *hūṃ*.
One should visualize [the victim] being devoured by Vajrayakṣa after having been struck down.
Having reflected upon the food,
[one should consume it] with the form of the Wrathful One (*krodha*) of *hūṃbhuva*, together with the vajra.
Some enter this mandala seeking the accomplishment of mantras;
others do so desiring merit, while still others seek the welfare of the next world.
A wise person, having directed their intention toward the next world and having cultivated great faith, should enter the maṇḍala; they should not seek any fruit pertaining to this world.

For one who desires the fruits of this world, the results pertaining to the next world are not so great; however, for a man seeking the sake of the next world, the fruit of this world is indeed abundant.

Having drawn those disciples in by means of the rays of light from the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva) residing in one’s own heart, having caused them to enter one’s own body through the gateway of the mouth, having transformed them into the form of lunar liquid, and having expelled them through the path of the vajra, one should visualize them as being consecrated by the bodhicitta-liquids consisting of the Tathāgatas who are the lotuses of the Vidyās appearing as one’s own reflections. Then, sitting at the gate of the maṇḍala, one should make this request: "O [Lord], you who appear as my own reflection! You are my teacher, O Great Hero, joined in union with Māmakī."
O Great Lord, I desire this firm method of great awakening.
Grant me the commitment; grant me the reality and the bodhicitta.
Grant me the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the Three Refuges. O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.
By this, having made one disciple the principal [recipient].
"Come, child! I shall correctly teach you the ritual procedure for the way of mantra practice in the Mahāyāna; you are a worthy vessel for the Great Vehicle."
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras.
By means of this incomparable application of mantra,
the exceedingly terrible and mighty army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having conformed to worldly custom and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained nirvana;
therefore, my child, apply your mind to this for the sake of attaining omniscience.

Thus the preceptor should cause them to hear. Thereafter, having caused them to recite the verse beginning with “The Three Jewels are my refuge,” and having touched their hearts, throats, and heads with the vajra, he should visualize upon moon-maṇḍalas on lotus petals the syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, as well as white, red, and black wheels, lotuses, and vajras. Furthermore, he should place those same seed-syllables in their centers. Having transformed all of that, he should install Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya in the form of three-faced, six-armed deities. Thereafter, he should sprinkle them with water from a flask held in hands joined with the bell and vajra.

Afterwards, having offered flowers upon their heads, perfume to their hearts, incense before them, water for the feet at their feet, and water for rinsing the mouth in their hands, and having consecrated it with the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī* mantra, he should give to the disciples a tooth-stick made of *aśvattha* or other such wood—one that is not fallen [from a tree], free of blemishes, one span in length, provided with young shoots, and adorned with a flower garland. Those disciples, having taken it, stand on ground smeared to the measure of a cow-hide, facing either east or north, and after chewing it, they cast it away. One should know that the highest accomplishment belongs to him toward whom it falls; or, if it falls [in a certain direction], it should be known from that. Regarding food, it should be known...?
Likewise, with the tip pointing eastward, middling accomplishment is proclaimed.
Likewise, if [the tooth-stick] faces upward, success in the world beyond is considered to occur.
However, a tooth-stick thrown in may sometimes fall face downward.
Then the attainment of the underworld (pātāla) shall certainly occur; there is no doubt about this.
% NB Guhyatantra verses Thereafter, one should give three handfuls of scented water contained in a lotus vessel or a conch shell to the disciples for rinsing the mouth:
*oṃ hrīḥ viśuddhadharma sarvapāpāni cāsya viśodhaya sarvavikalpān apanaya hūṃ*.

Having made them drink with this [mixture], one should have them rinse their mouths. Having seated them once again, one should give them *kuśa* grass consecrated with the *Amṛtakuṇḍalin* mantra for the purpose of a rug and a pillow.

Thereafter, having tied a red-colored thread—triple-stranded and knotted three times—with a mantra consecrated by the Vighnāri-mantra around the arms of the disciples for their protection, one should encourage them to listen to the teaching of the Dharma.
Do omniscient beings ever appear in the world, or not? They may appear only once in a great while, like the flower of the udumbara tree.
Even rarer than that is the arising of the way of mantra practice,
by which those who do not pass into nirvana are indeed able to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings.
Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons,
all of that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala.
The miserable states of existence, which are the source of all suffering,
are destroyed for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme conduct.
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains,
in that you are here in this teaching as true sons of all the Victors.
All those who are born are received by great-souled beings along with their mothers;
therefore, you shall indeed be well-born and great-souled.
"O children, will you become so?
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna,
by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas."
Having thus caused them to hear this teaching of the Dharma, and having protected them with the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra, one should cause them to take the special vow.
O Lord, having bestowed the irreversible consecration of the wheel,
please tell me the reality of the wheel and its deity, as well as the preparatory rites for the master.
"I shall always be the preceptor for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings; [this is] the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow."
He should have those disciples sleep upon a bed of kuśa grass, saying: "Whatever you see in a dream, you shall tell me in the morning.
This is the ritual procedure for the consecration of the disciples.
Having entered the maṇḍala hall, one should recite the *kuṇḍalī* mantra for the sake of protection.
Having offered the *bali*, at dawn one should summon the disciple and question him.
Furthermore, the preceptor effects protection against inauspiciousness by means of the Kuṇḍalī-mantras;
or else, through a fire-oblation (homa), he shall then declare auspiciousness for the favorable occasion.

Then, having performed a grand worship upon the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) or other mandala, the preceptor himself, preceded by the worship of his own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), enters the mandala according to the ritual for the entry of disciples. He should then obtain, through the mental presence of the Lord Adhipati, the consecrations to be described up to the final authorization (*anujñā*).
Immediately thereafter, he should pray to Vajrasattva for the sake of admitting the disciples.
All phenomena are like reflections: transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet arise from causes and karma.
"By the truth that [the mandala] has emerged from the reality of suchness,
may all the disciples, free from stain, behold the mandala clearly as a reflection."

Having made such requests as these, [the master] should ask the disciple—who has been given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) outside the curtain (kāṇḍapaṭa), who is visualized in the form of Vairocana, who holds a flower garland with the mantra *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, and whose eyes are bound with a blindfold and who has been sprinkled with water from the vase—for the purpose of entering the maṇḍala: "Who are you, O lover of delight (*ratipriya*)? [The disciple replies] with the words beginning with "I am...
and so forth.
He should say: "I am fortunate; I am great bliss.
Having placed the vajra upon the heart of the disciple, he should speak thus:
"Oṃ, I generate the mind of vajra-yoga. O Surata, you are the pledge (samaya). Hoḥ! Accomplished one, vajra, great bliss!"
Having thus generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should speak as follows:

"Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas. You must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to anyone who has not entered the maṇḍala, nor should it be revealed to those lacking faith. Then, having summoned [the disciple] with the mantra *hūṃ jaḥ hūṃ*, and having led them inside the curtain and established them at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, one should speak thus.

Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the vajra-knowledge, by means of which knowledge you will attain even the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated through the failure to avoid misfortune.
Again, placing the vajra upon the head, one should speak thus:
"This is your samaya-vajra; it shall split your head if you speak of it to anyone."
Having placed a vajra with flowers [upon it], one should say:
"Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself is now established within your heart;
he would depart at that very moment, piercing through [it], if you were to speak of this method."
One should certainly say this, though it is seen elsewhere that,

having caused [the person] to swear an oath, one should produce the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) placed in a lotus vessel, empowered by the three syllables, and generated through the sequence beginning with the moon and the vajra. Having recited *oṃ vajrāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ* seven times, one should have [the person] drink it with this verse.
This water of yours is hellish; it shall burn you if you transgress the pledge. Through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment; drink this vajra-amṛta water!
Having recited this and made [the disciple] drink [the water], the following should be said:

"From this day forward, I, Vajrapāṇi, am your master; whatever I tell you to do must be performed by you, and you must not disregard me. Lest, by failing to avoid misfortune, you should meet your end and fall into hell."
The offering of water according to the pledge. [Vajra] ||
Then, one should cause a single disciple to recite:
"May all the Tathāgatas empower me; may Vajrasattva enter me!
Then, upon the head [of the disciple], there is a white Varuṇa-maṇḍala, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, marked with a water-pot, circular, and empowered by the syllable *haḥ*.

Then, one should meditate on a yellow square earth-maṇḍala marked with a three-pronged vajra, transformed from the syllable *laṃ*, at the heart; a blue *hūṃ* at the throat; and at the soles of the feet, a triangular fire-maṇḍala blazing with garlands of radiating rays and accompanied by light, transformed from the syllable *raṃ*, marked with a fluttering banner, and presided over by the syllable *yaṃ*, which is the wind-maṇḍala. Having visualized this, it is ignited by the wind-maṇḍala. *Jhaiḥ* (with rays). Meditating thus...
Having placed the *samayavaṭikā* in the mouth and holding the incense burner, while sounding the bell with a majestic air,
one should utter: "Oṃ rama ramattaṃ ṅga vājjasatta samayam anupālaya hūṃ."
Having uttered "ĀVEŚAYA STOBHAYA SAVAYA HŪṂ HAḤ ĀḤ JHAIḤ," one should visualize on the tongue a red syllable *ĀḤ* transformed into a vajra-tongue in the form of Amitābha, and say:
"O child, speak what is auspicious."
He should say this. Having understood what was said, he should utter, "Stay, O Vajra; become firm," and place a vajra upon his heart. He should then ask again.
"What kind of appearance does your eye have?

Then, having determined whether [the disciple] is fit for pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāru*), or auspiciousness (*bhavyatā*) based on the white, yellow, red, green, or black appearances described by him, one should perform the empowerment through truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*):
"Thus, this disciple has been properly introduced into the maṇḍala by me."
May the lineage of the deities remain exactly as it is meritorious.
Whatever kind of accomplishment may arise for him, in whatever lineage and in whatever vessel;
and whatever the power of the merit of the food and the vessel may be— may such [power] belong to this mandala.
Then, one should cast that flower garland into the mandala with the mantra: "Pratīccha vajra hoh."
Then, by the falling of the flower, one should discern whether the accomplishment (siddhi) is inferior or superior.

In that regard, if it falls upon the head, the *uṣṇīṣa*, or the forehead of the Buddhas, then there is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. If it falls upon the mouth or the eyes, then there is the accomplishment of Mantra. Furthermore, if it falls on the upper part of the body, the result is superior; if on the middle part of the body, the result is middling.
Success is attained slowly when far from the image, and quickly when near it.
When near, the quick success of the deities is to be understood by the division of their respective locations, such as the central chamber and so forth.
If it falls between two deities, then it belongs to whichever deity's flower is closer;
if it falls outside the mandala, there is a minor accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*).
If it falls upon the lines, one should cast it again.
In that very case, there is no accomplishment if one falls in three ways:
there is no accomplishment if one falls outside the outer row of vajras;
it is even more difficult [to attain accomplishment] if one falls inside the womb.
Then, having brought him outside with that very blindfold and removed it, he should address the disciples with the mantra and other recitations beginning with "Oṃ."
Because of their evil conduct, one should subsequently cause them all to undergo [the rites] as previously described.
This is the procedure for the casting of flowers (puṣpapātana).
Then, having taken that garland once more, he should bind it upon the head of the disciple while reciting:
"Accept this, O child, O Mahābala!
Having meditated on Kṣitigarbha through the transformation of the *oṃ* syllable into a wheel at the two eyes.
Oṃ! Vajrasattva, today intent upon opening your eyes, the Vajra-Eyed One opens for you the unsurpassed Vajra-eye.
He should remove the blindfold.

Then, preceded by a prostration with eight limbs, one should display the maṇḍala circle. In the center is Akṣobhya, whose intrinsic nature is consciousness (*vijñāna*). In the east is Vairocana, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); in feeling (*vedanā*) is Ratnasaṃbhava; in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is Amitābha; and in formations (*saṃskāra*) is Amoghasiddhi. In the corners beginning with the southeast, there are Locanā and the others through the purification of earth, water, fire, and air. Through the purification of the objects of sense, there are Rūpavajrā and the others. Through the purification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, there are Yamāntaka and the others. Through the purification of the sense faculties, there are Kṣitigarbha and the others. This is the procedure for entering the maṇḍala.
Now the consecration is described:
"Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by the Bodhivajra,
so too, for the sake of my protection, O Khavajra, grant it to me today."
With this [verse], he should request the guru.

Thereafter, the preceptor, having visualized the disciple as being supported by the form of Akṣobhya and emerged from the joy of the Vidyā-puruṣa, and having taken him by the hand with the vajra, shall rise and sprinkle him with water from the flask using a mango sprout:
"The great vajra consecration, honored by the three realms..."
I bestow [this] which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Vajra Lord;
[I sprinkle] the disciple seated upon an auspicious throne, like a universal monarch, with raised parasols, banners, flags, and so forth. One should thus sprinkle him.
The water consecration is the mirror-like wisdom.

Then, with the consecration verse, one should place upon the disciple’s head a crown fashioned from gold, cloth, and other materials, through the yoga of Ratnasambhava. All the Tathāgatas residing in the expanse of space should be visualized within the crown in the form of the Lord of the Family.
This is the crown consecration, which is the wisdom of equality.
Having placed the great nine-pronged vajra upon the heart with his hand,
he should sprinkle the disciple— who has the form of Lokeśvara— with the eye of Vajrasattva.
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration;
take this vajra of all the Buddhas for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
Reciting thus, and having touched [the disciple] on the head, heart, and other parts, one should place the vajra in the right hand.
This is the vajra-consecration, which is the wisdom of discerning observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Then, having visualized oneself in the form of Amoghasiddhi and placed a bell in the left hand, one should perform the gesture of embracing with both hands joined by the vajra and bell, and recite: "Oṃ, O Lord of Vajras, I consecrate you; abide as the Vajra!"
The bell initiation is the gnosis of the performance of activities.
Having visualized the disciple as Vairocana, one should consecrate him by name. Placing the vajra and the bell upon his head, [the preceptor] should [consecrate him] with this verse:

"Oṃ, O Vajrasattva, I consecrate you through the vajra-name-consecration; O Śrī Dveṣavajra! and so forth, according to the tradition of the Buddhas. Furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should assign a name in accordance with the [disciple's] family (kula).
The consecration of the name "Knowledge of the Perfectly Pure Dharmadhātu."
By means of these consecrations, one becomes authorized for hearing and explaining the mantra-tantras, as well as for the practice of mantras.
The fivefold consecration alone is called the *vidyābhiṣeka* (wisdom-consecration), because of the activity of Locanā and the other goddesses in all cases.
Immediately after that:
"O treasure of compassion, grant me the master’s initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka),
so that by your grace I may become capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others."
Thus did the disciple, adorned with all ornaments,
and accompanied by raised variegated banners, flags, yak-tail whisks, and parasols, make his request.
In the east, the Holder of the Vajra, assuming the form of Vajrasattva, should take hold of the disciple who is seated upon a lion throne and adorned with canopies and musical instruments.
Having meditated on [the deity] born from the *vajra-jah-hūṃ* syllable, one should place it in the hand while reciting this:
"The being without beginning or end is Vajrasattva, the Great Joy."
One should cause [the disciple] to grasp the reality that the Blessed One is Samantabhadra, the self of all, the Lord of Vajragarbha, the primordial Supreme Person.
Following that, the realization of the mudrās is taught: one whose mental form possesses firm vows has a firm embodiment of all [deities]; because of this, they are proclaimed as "mudrās."
In the form of one's own chosen deity, however, one should effect the embrace of one's own mudrā.
Immediately after that, having visualized the disciple being consecrated by the hosts of deities who have emerged from the heart of the preceptor and are stationed in the sky:
[The preceptor bestows] the great vajra-consecration, which is venerated by the three realms.
I bestow [this] which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas.
One should perform the consecration with the *avaivartika-gāthā*. Thus it is said in the *Śrī-samāja*:
"Embracing with both hands a Prajñā sixteen years of age, through the union of the bell and the vajra, this is considered the consecration of the Ācārya."
Thereafter, one should explain the reality of the mandala and the purification of the mandala according to their enumeration. "Maṇḍa" is said to be the essence; it is the bodhicitta of great bliss.
Because it takes that [essence] up, the mandala is considered to be the gathering (mīlana).
The "pinnacle chamber" (kūṭāgāra) is said to be the pinnacle, which is the elevation of the mind;
the five aggregates (skandhas), in brief, are proclaimed as the five Buddhas.
Thus concludes the purification of the mandala.
Then, one should grant the authorization to the disciple who has been focused upon in the form of Vairocana and the other [deities]:
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way,
turn the wheel of Dharma everywhere according to the needs of those to be trained."
By casting a vajra, a jewel, or a sword into the place of the Dharma,
permission is granted through the recitation of this verse four times.
Then,
having focused upon the form of Akṣobhya, one should bestow the vow:
"This is that state of all Buddhas, which resides in the hand of Vajrasattva."
For you, too, must always maintain the firm vow of Vajrapāṇi.

With this [mantra], one should give the vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Reciting: *oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhivajrasamaye tiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should cause the disciple to grasp the vajra.
This is the bestowal of the vajra vow (*vajravratadāna*).

Thereafter, having meditated upon oneself as the form of the Buddha, and having taken the corner of the robe with the left fist at the heart, one should form the boon-granting mudrā with the right hand and instruct the family; one should perform the prophecy in that very form.
I, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, prophesy for you this:
having extracted you from the miserable states of existence, for the sake of ultimate purification from cyclic existence.
"O Tathāgata named [Amuka]vajra, you are the one who has attained the samaya of siddhi; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar. Thus he should pronounce the prophecy. This is the prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
Thereafter, reciting "Mahāsamaya hana hūṃ phaṭ," one should give the breath of reassurance:
"Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today indeed liberated from all sins and well-established."
There is no further death for you from this Great Bliss Vehicle;
your suffering of existence has been extinguished for the sake of ultimate purification from becoming.
Until the end of the suffering of existence,
the *bodhicitta* born of all yoginīs must certainly not be abandoned.
By the mere production of which one becomes a Buddha, without a doubt.
The true Dharma is never to be rejected nor ever abandoned;
however, one should not explain it out of ignorance or delusion.
The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā must never be abandoned;
the ācārya must not be disparaged, for he is equal to all the Buddhas.
Having renounced one's own self, one should not afflict oneself with austerities;
happiness should be maintained at ease, for this one is a fully awakened Buddha yet to come.
Thus ends the consolation.

And these four, beginning with the permission (anujñā), are bestowed either immediately after the five empowerments or immediately after the master empowerment (ācāryābhiṣeka). The master empowerment itself is called the irreversible empowerment (avaivartikābhiṣeka). Thus, the six empowerments—the five empowerments plus the master empowerment—are not contradicted in any of the tantras.

NB: Vāgīśvarakīrti states: These four, beginning with *anujñā* (permission), are bestowed either immediately after the fifth consecration or after the fourth consecration. The *ācāryābhiṣeka* (master consecration) alone is called the *avaivartikābhiṣeka* (consecration of non-retrogression). The five consecrations consist of the *ācāryābhiṣeka* and the *kalaśābhiṣeka* (vase consecration), because in all cases the vases are employed. These six consecrations are not contradictory even in the *Kriyātantra*, as they are seen in the *Mañjuśrītantra* and other such texts.
The six empowerments... [there is likely a scribal eye-skip here].
Then, by means of the master empowerment (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), the vajra-body (*kāyavajra*) is purified.

% THE SECRET INITIATION % [Note the parallels with Vāgīśvarakīrti throughout! Thereafter, in a place made secluded by means of a curtain or similar screen, the disciple—having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth a consort (prajñā) who is pleasing to his own mind, endowed with beauty and youth, capable of observing the pledges and vows, sixteen years of age, of auspicious appearance, and not yet having borne children—and having offered her to the Guru, presented betel, fragrant flowers, and other offerings, and prostrated; then, having gone outside, he should make this request:
Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra,
so too, for the sake of my protection, O Khavajra, grant it to me today!

GST 16.58 = GMV 323: The Guru, having accepted her and made her into a *pañcakula-kalāpinī* (one possessing the five families), and having performed the embrace and so forth preceded by the cultivation of the three absorptions (*samādhi*), visualizes a red syllable *hrīṃ* on the tip of his left index finger; having cast her into the *dharmadhātu*, he should move her like a full moon.
Then, for the sake of equal bliss, having inserted the *vajra* into the lotus and experienced bliss, [he remains] in the state of liberation.
Having bound the bliss of wisdom and likewise the bliss of means,
whatever is performed there through service should be cast into the mouth of the disciple.
Whether it be the disciple or the two lotuses in the form of the vajra, he should drink while reciting: "Aho! Great Bliss!"
Thus, through the secret empowerment, there is the purification of the speech-vajra.
% THE CONSECRATION OF WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE % Observe the parallels with Vāgīśvarakīrti!!!

According to the system of the Single Seal (*ekamudrā*), it should be performed with that very [consort]; according to the system of the Differentiated Seals (*bhinnamudrā*), it should be performed with another [consort] endowed with similar characteristics. In that very context, for the sake of demonstrating the *dharmakāya*—which is to be personally realized by each individual—it must be brought into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the sphere of the disciple.

Having been requested by the disciple with the verse beginning "By the Bodhi-vajra of the Buddhas," [the master], having placed his own hand upon the disciple's hand and having made the beings who have come from the various realms bear witness, [proceeds].
Having placed a vajra upon the heads of all the Tathāgatas, it is spoken by the Guru-vajrī:
This delightful dhāraṇī, revealed by the Buddhas, is to be cultivated;
through the application of the sequence of the wheel, experience the true bliss.

Buddhahood is not attained by any other means, and these three worlds are pure; therefore, with a mind intent on separation [from defilements], you should never entertain any longing for anything else.
This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
for the fool who transgresses it, there shall be no supreme accomplishment.
Thus one should give.

She too, her limbs smeared with saffron and sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands of flowers, being naked, should sit in the *utkuṭaka* posture and clearly display her own lotus; she should speak as follows.
[She said:
"O fierce one, are you clearly manifesting [your intent]? But, my child, are you able to consume feces, urine, and the like?"
Tell me, my child, as you please: [the nature of] blood, semen, and likewise flesh; the supreme devotion of women, and furthermore, the kissing of the lotus of the womb.
Thus he too would say.
Moreover, O Queen, I cannot bring myself to consume semen, blood, and the like;
rather, women should always be honored through kissing and indeed through sexual union.
Then, joyful and gazing with love at the face of the practitioner as if he were her beloved, she should say:
"Oh, my lotus is endowed with all happiness;
for him who serves it according to the prescribed rite, I stand before him."
O Padmā, perform whatever task is required, such as the propitiation of the Perfectly Awakened One;
for the King Mahāsukha himself is established right here.
"Enjoy me! O one who desires liberation!

Thus the disciple, whose self is united with his own tutelary deity, places the five-syllable *kulakalāpinī*—*oṃ āḥ hūṃ svā hā*—respectively upon her head, heart, navel, secret place, and the pair of thighs. With the syllable *hūṃ*, he should visualize a lotus and a vajra; with *oṃ*, a lotus and a varataka (a type of seed-pod); and with *āḥ*, the filaments of the lotus, as well as the moon and the lotus itself. [He should visualize] the yellow *phaṭ*-syllable. Having touched the navel of Vajradhātvīśvarī with the tip of his index finger, he should perform the consecration of the lotus by uttering the sound *śī* three times.
Oṃ! O support of the bliss of the lotus, great passion, grant me bliss!
You who speak of the four joys, hūṃ hūṃ, perform my task!
She also performed the empowerment with the vajra:
*Oṃ vajramahādveṣa caturānandadāyaka khagamukhaikaraso nātha hūṃ 2 kuruṣva me kāryam*.

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Anurāga-navajra of all Tathāgatas. Having inserted the vajra into the lotus and having made all the Lords of Jinas witnesses here, and so forth, according to the words of the Buddha. (Witnesses: *sākṣiṇaḥ*)
Furthermore, it is said that one should practice through the union of wisdom and means;
from the conjunction of the vajra and the lotus, it is called the "near-attainment" (upasādhana).
The accomplishment is declared to be the shaking [of the body], accompanied by the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.

When that which is inherently existent, blissful, and peaceful occurs, then it is innate joy (*sahajānanda*). Thus it is said: "The outflow (*niṣyanda*) is said to be at the navel; the maturation (*vipāka*) is at the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*); the virile power (*puruṣakāra*) is at the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhoga*); and the state of stainlessness (*vaimalya*) resides in great bliss (*mahāsukha*)."

This concludes the ritual procedure for initiation (*sekaprakriyā*) according to the *Kālacakra*, which constitutes initiation according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*). This is because of the statement: "It is sevenfold, threefold, tenfold, and the fourth is likewise. Thus, the fourth is the supramundane initiation (*lokottarābhiṣeka*). Regarding the statement that "the third is the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and the fourth does not exist," it follows from the statement "the fourth is the knowledge of wisdom; that again is likewise" that the fourth is indeed the knowledge of wisdom.
It is stated in the Kālacakra:
Note: Quote the *Kālacakra*! Note the variants:

"The touching of the breasts of the Prajñā, as well as the tasting and beholding of the nectar, would occur; and upon union with the Prajñā, when the bodhicitta has melted, there is the fourth moment, which has reached the state of nectar."
All that is indeed mundane, shown for the sake of the path through supreme compassion;
whereas the supramundane consecration, O Lord of the Supreme Victors, is that which is associated with the divine mudrās.

Having abandoned this stained mental construct of the *karmamudrā*, one should, for the sake of perfect enlightenment, meditate upon the *divyamudrā*, the mother of the supreme Victors, who is the *jñānamudrā*.

Untainted, changeless, having destroyed the darkness of impurity, all-pervading, attainable through yoga, immutable, the light of knowledge, the remover of the defilement of worldly existence, and interwoven with the wheel of time.

The mere appearance of the mind, produced within one's own consciousness like a reflection in a mirror, is indeed to be cultivated by the lords of yoga; it is that which has been practiced by all the sons of the Victors and by the Buddhas.
Awakened by the flame of gnosis, she burns the entire host of Māra together with its objects;
and through the yoga of the rain, she bestows equal bliss upon the bodies of yogins regarding passion and the rest.

Wisdom (*prajñā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and mind (*citta*) become tenfold; their mere appearance is the consecration (*seka*) in this [teaching], which is indeed like the reflection in a mirror resembling the stainless moon.
Therefore, he whose heart possesses this fourth state— the innate, imperishable, and unfallen bliss of nirvāṇa, which is the very mouth of the Buddha— is the glorious Guru.
With minds unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the path of the vajra,
from emptiness there arise smoke, a mirage, a glow-worm in the clear sky, and a lamp.

Even the flames, moon, sun, and vajras are seen as the supreme digit, and within that, the drop (*bindu*) appears as the universal image (*viśvabimba*), the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* free from sense objects.
With a steady gaze upon the sky, free from clouds— there is nothing else but the mind itself.
When the image has been seen, one should perform the restraint of the vital breath at every daily occasion,
until indeed a circle of light rays, revolving and encircling one's own body, is perceived. Within six months, the path-consciousness of the ascetics— which is devoid of touch— attains equal bliss.
That moment, which marks the end of passion and its absence, increases by the number of breaths for the Lord.
The secret [bliss] is within the interval of the flames; between innate knowledge and discernment;
sleep at the junction of the whirlpools; and that bliss which arises from the union of the pair of the vajra and the lotus.

His increase shall proceed by virtue of the guru’s strict injunctions; there is nothing surprising in this, for that yogi, having slain the afflictions and the Māras, enters the state of the Lord of Jinas through the yoga of the year.
The nature of the earth is firm, not having the form of flowing water; it is not liquid because it lacks fluidity.

Having the form of fire yet not fire; having the body of wind yet being motionless and not wind; appearing as emptiness yet visible; possessing white, green, and great variegated colors yet not a color;
having all forms yet not visible—this is due to the turbidity of one's own heart through the power of the Māra of the afflictions.
Nāda, bindu, kalā, and jñāna are the chains; the channels proceed to the plane of the nectar.
Prāṇa and apāna are the three paths; the vajra together with the lotus is indeed the vajra joined with the lotus.
The sounding of the bell within the drum, the exit and entry of the objects and the subjects,
the sign of the smoke and so forth, and also whatever grasping there may be— all this is the secret.

In the center, there is the entry of the vital breath; the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left channels; the mind, through engagement with the mudrā, having attained supreme bliss; and the awakening of the vajra.
The awakening by means of the vajra,

or the sound of the vajra within the lotus, or else the splashing of water from the palms for the sake of pleasure, the emission of the seed-syllable for one's own bliss— this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which removes the fear of death.
The earth dissolves into water, and water likewise into fire; and the wind [dissolves] into fire.
By means of the practice of this yoga, whether by a woman or a man,
supreme bliss is enjoyed for as long as twelve years.
That bliss by which those born in this cycle of existence experience death,
and yet again birth and even stability— that bliss is called meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Thus ends the consecration of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), according to Hevajra I.iii.21cd.
